title: Odometry Calibration for a Differential-Drive Public Service Robot at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang

authors.name: Dr. Agus Prabowo
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Universitas Diponegoro

abstract: We propose an odometry calibration pipeline for a differential-drive public service robot deployed at Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang. Routine use in hospital corridors reveals systematic drift due to wheel radius asymmetry and wheelbase uncertainty, causing translational and rotational errors that compromise navigation for tasks such as medication delivery and patient escorting. The proposed calibration module combines model-based odometry correction, a constrained nonlinear least-squares estimator, and an online parameter update executed at 50 Hz. Extensive experiments conducted in real hospital corridors with a test dataset of 1 200 runs demonstrate that our method reduces translational RMSE from 0.462 m to 0.124 m and rotational drift from 2.6 deg/m to 0.70 deg/m. The proposed approach achieves overall localization accuracy of 95.4% in corridor tracking tasks while operating on an onboard Intel NUC with latency 12.3 ms, outperforming baseline methods. The main contributions of this work are: (i) a practical calibration workflow adapted to hospital environments; (ii) a robust cost function for joint estimation of wheel radii and wheelbase; and (iii) a validation on-site at Wongsonegoro Hospital demonstrating significant accuracy and reliability improvements.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Hospital service robots are increasingly adopted for logistic tasks such as medication delivery, transport of small equipment, and patient guidance. In these real-world settings, accurate localization and path following are essential to ensure safety and timeliness, especially in crowded corridors and constrained spaces. Differential-drive mobile robots remain popular due to mechanical simplicity and low cost, but odometry errors accumulate rapidly over distance because of wheel radius variations, misestimated wheelbase, encoder resolution limits, and surface interactions. In this paper we present a field-deployable calibration method specifically tailored for a public service robot operating at Wongsonegoro Hospital in Semarang, Indonesia, where corridor geometry and operational constraints require practical, low-overhead solutions.

Prior work has addressed odometry modeling and calibration using a variety of techniques. Classic closed-form corrections and least-squares regression [1][2] reduce systematic bias but often assume laboratory conditions and symmetric wheels, which is unrealistic for long-term deployed robots. Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) fusion of odometry with intermittent absolute measurements improves robustness yet depends on reliable external references [3][4]. Recent data-driven approaches using machine learning provide flexibility [5][6] but require large labeled datasets and substantial compute. Despite achieving good results in controlled settings, prior work suffers from limited field validation in busy institutional environments and lacks an integrated workflow bridging offline calibration and online parameter updates during routine operations.

The practical challenge at Wongsonegoro Hospital is twofold: first, the robot exhibits consistent translational bias caused by asymmetric wheel radii and slightly mismeasured wheelbase $b$; second, rotational drift accumulates during turns and long straight runs. Existing vendor calibration utilities provided with the robot were insufficient because they assume uniform floor friction and laboratory alignment, leading to residual errors that degrade task execution. To address this challenge, we introduce a combined offline and online calibration procedure that estimates the parameter vector $p= [b, r_L, r_R]$ where $r_L$ and $r_R$ are left and right wheel radii, respectively, and $b$ is the effective wheel separation used in the odometry model.

We propose a novel practical pipeline, OdometryCal-WG (Wongsonegoro Guided calibration), which is designed to operate within hospital constraints and integrates into the robot's existing software stack. The proposed method is robust to measurement noise, uses minimal specialized equipment (a tape measure and ground-truth waypoints), and is executed at 50 Hz to allow on-the-fly adaptation. The main contributions of this work are:

1) We propose OdometryCal-WG, a novel approach to joint estimation of wheel radii and wheelbase using constrained nonlinear least-squares tailored for in-situ hospital corridors.
2) The proposed calibration module is designed to run on modest edge hardware (Intel NUC), performing online updates and yielding real-time corrected odometry at low latency.
3) Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method reduces translational RMSE to 0.124 m and rotational drift to 0.70 deg/m, achieving 95.4% overall localization accuracy and outperforming common baselines by 4.1–8.3% in accuracy metrics.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on odometry calibration, sensor fusion, and field-deployable methods. Section III describes the system design and the proposed calibration algorithm, including mathematical modeling and implementation details. Section IV presents experimental setup, datasets, quantitative results, ablation studies, and comparison with existing methods. Section V concludes with a discussion of limitations and directions for future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section synthesizes literature across odometry correction, encoder-based calibration, and field deployment of mobile robots. We provide focused subsections on classical model-based calibration, filter-based fusion, and machine learning approaches with particular emphasis on methods that have been validated in real environments [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].

content.text: Classical methods model wheel encoder integration using kinematic equations and perform parameter identification via least-squares or total least-squares methods [1][2]. These approaches explicitly model wheel radius $r$ and wheelbase $b$, and estimate biases such as slip coefficients. Notably, Borenstein and Feng proposed calibration schemes for mobile robots that estimate effective wheel radii and baseline using straight and turning maneuvers [9]. More recent model-based work applies constrained optimization to jointly estimate multiple parameters under physical bounds [10][11]. These methods are computationally efficient and interpretable, but despite their theoretical appeal, they often assume idealized planar motion and controlled conditions, making direct application to hospital corridors challenging where surface variance and narrow corridors produce additional disturbances. In our work we adopt the model-based perspective but augment it with online updates and practical data collection procedures that are suitable for Wongsonegoro Hospital operations [1][2][9].

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the typical model-based calibration pipeline connects encoder measurements to a parameter estimator that outputs corrected odometry. Prior work [10][11] has emphasized the importance of parameter identifiability and experiment design; we adopt these lessons by selecting trajectories in hospital corridors that excite both translational and rotational degrees of freedom while maintaining patient safety.

Filter-based approaches, including EKF and unscented Kalman filters (UKF), fuse odometry with absolute or relative measurements (e.g., LiDAR, UWB, visual landmarks) to bound drift [3][4][12]. These techniques have been widely adopted in service robots for hospitals and warehouses due to their robustness and real-time properties. However, EKF-based solutions rely on accurate process and observation models and often treat odometry errors as zero-mean noise, which understates systematic biases arising from permanently misestimated $r_L$ and $r_R$. Our method complements filter-based fusion by first reducing systematic bias in raw odometry through explicit parameter estimation, thereby improving the assumptions on which a filter relies and reducing residual covariance during sensor fusion.

For example, the Kalman gain equation $K_k = P_k^{-} H^{T} (H P_k^{-} H^{T} + R)^{-1}$ captures how state uncertainty and observation noise interact [12]. By lowering odometry bias and reducing $P_k^{-}$ via improved odometry, downstream localization accuracy improves and filter convergence is faster. We incorporate such insights when designing experiments and when reporting improvements relative to EKF-only baselines [3][12].

Recent work applies machine learning to odometry correction using regression models or neural networks trained on paired odometry and ground truth sequences [5][6][13]. These methods can learn complex biases, including terrain-dependent effects, but typically require large labeled datasets and nontrivial compute resources. For hospital deployment, collecting ground truth over many corridor variations is operationally expensive and risks interrupting clinical activities. Lightweight learning approaches that augment physics-based models show promise [14], but their field-readiness for constrained hospital corridors has not been thoroughly demonstrated. Our approach favors an interpretable parameter estimation procedure with limited data requirements and low computational demands, making it practical for Wongsonegoro Hospital conditions while maintaining compatibility with occasional data-driven refinement.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the robot platform at Wongsonegoro Hospital, the kinematic odometry model, the calibration cost function, and the implementation of the OdometryCal-WG pipeline running on embedded edge hardware.

content.text: The system architecture integrates the onboard STM32 microcontroller, an Intel NUC edge computer, wheel encoders AS5048, a DRV8301 motor driver, and a hospital Map Server that provides corridor maps and waypoints. As presented in Table I, the robot has nominal wheel radius $r=0.075$ m and an initial wheelbase estimate $b=0.48$ m. As shown in Fig. 2, the architecture consists of encoder data acquisition at 500 Hz on the MCU, downsampled to 50 Hz for the Odometry Estimator on the NUC, and an optional Map Server providing ground-truth waypoints. The proposed calibration module receives sequences of encoder increments and sparse ground-truth displacements and produces updated parameters $p= [b, r_L, r_R]$ which are then applied to the low-level odometry computation module. Communication between modules uses MQTT with TLS over 802.11ac, keeping latency low and secure.

content.text: The proposed module is designed to be modular: it accepts logged encoder sequences, optional ground truth waypoints from the Map Server, and outputs updated parameters that are propagated back to the low-level odometry node. Safety and clinical compatibility were prioritized; calibration runs are performed during low-traffic hours in corridor sections approved by hospital staff.

Equation (1) is the standard first-order approximation for odometry pose update where $x, y$ updates use trapezoidal integration through $\\Delta s$ and $\\Delta\\theta$. In our implementation $x$ represents the pose vector $[x, y, \\theta]^{T}$ and $\\Delta s_k$ is the forward displacement during the $k$-th interval. The use of the mid-angle $\\theta_k + \\Delta\\theta_k/2$ reduces integration error for moderate angular rates. This formula is robust and computationally cheap for 50 Hz operation.

The hardware used at Wongsonegoro Hospital is summarized in Table I and illustrated in Fig. 3. The on-robot computing stack comprises an STM32F407 MCU responsible for real-time encoder reading and PWM generation, and an Intel NUC for higher-level perception, odometry estimation, and calibration optimization. Wheel encoders are magnetic AS5048 rotary encoders with resolution $N_{enc}=4096$ ticks per revolution. The motor driver is DRV8301 interfacing with BLDC motors rated 100 W. The battery is a 24 V 12 Ah sealed lead-acid pack that powers the drive and the onboard electronics via a 5 V regulator. Mechanical parameters were measured with calipers and tape measures before calibration, yielding nominal $r=0.075$ m and $b=0.48$ m. The hardware choices prioritize robustness and maintainability in a hospital environment.

Table I lists the specific hardware and measured mechanical parameters used during experiments. The measured encoder resolution $N_{enc}=4096$ informs the tick-to-angle conversion and is used in all kinematic formulas. The hardware setup was installed and tested in corridor sections approved by hospital staff and is representative of routine service robot configurations in similar institutions.

content.text: We model the differential-drive wheel encoder increments as the fundamental measurements. Encoder ticks are converted to incremental wheel angles $\\Delta\\phi_{L}$ and $\\Delta\\phi_{R}$ using the known resolution $N_{enc}$. The conversion formula used in implementation is $\\Delta\\phi = \frac{2\\pi\\Delta n}{N_{enc}}$. The proposed calibration estimates distinct left and right radii $r_L$ and $r_R$ as well as effective wheelbase $b$ by minimizing residuals between observed ground-truth displacements and predicted odometry. The algorithm is a two-stage process: an offline batch calibration for initial parameter estimates and an online constrained update running during routine operations to adapt to slow variations such as tire wear or floor conditions. The algorithm description below uses inline math for clarity: $b$ denotes wheelbase, $r_L$ and $r_R$ denote left and right wheel radii, and $\\Delta n$ denotes encoder tick increments.

Equation (2) generalizes the symmetric-wheel model by allowing different radii $r_L$ and $r_R$. The left and right incremental displacements are $s_L = r_L \\Delta\\phi_L$ and $s_R = r_R \\Delta\\phi_R$, and the average forward displacement is $\\Delta s = (s_R + s_L)/2$. The angular increment $\\Delta\\theta$ depends inversely on $b$ and amplifies asymmetry between left and right displacements. These expressions are central to both the odometry update (1) and the calibration objective function.

Equation (3) is the encoder ticks to radians conversion used throughout the pipeline. Here $N_{enc}=4096$ for AS5048 encoders, and $\\Delta n$ is the signed tick increment measured over a sampling interval. Noise in $\\Delta n$ and quantization effects at low speeds are accounted for in the estimator covariance.

We formulate the calibration as the minimization of the cost function $J(p)$ in (4) where $p=[b, r_L, r_R]^{T}$, $z_i$ are observed ground-truth displacements for the $i$-th segment (measured with tape measure and corridor markers), $u_i$ is the recorded encoder sequence for that segment, $h(p,u_i)$ is the forward model that predicts displacement given parameters $p$ and encoder data $u_i$, and $R$ is a diagonal covariance representing measurement confidence. The proposed method uses Levenberg-Marquardt with box constraints to ensure physically plausible values $r_L, r_R \in [0.06, 0.09]$ m and $b \in [0.40, 0.55]$ m.

To improve robustness, we include Tikhonov regularization and an outlier rejection stage where residuals beyond 3 standard deviations are downweighted. The constrained nonlinear solver runs on the Intel NUC and typically converges in less than 2 s for batch sizes of 20 segments. After convergence the updated parameters are published to the odometry node which uses equation (1) and (2) with the new $p$.

content.latex: P_{k+1}^{-} = F_k P_k F_k^{T} + G_k Q G_k^{T}

content.text: For integration with an EKF-based localization module, we propagate covariance using (5), where $F_k$ is the state transition Jacobian derived from partial derivatives of equation (1), $G_k$ maps process noise $Q$ (encoder noise and slippage) into state space, and $P$ denotes state covariance. By reducing model bias through parameter updates, the odometry residuals shrink and $P_{k+1}^{-}$ is reduced, improving Kalman filter performance.

content.text: The integration layer coordinates data flows among the MCU, edge computer, and hospital Map Server. Encoder data is acquired at 500 Hz on the STM32 and published over MQTT at 50 Hz to the NUC where the calibration and odometry estimation run. The proposed system uses secure TLS connections and a simple topic hierarchy: /robot/encoders, /robot/odometry, /calibration/update. Data packets include timestamps and sequence numbers to allow out-of-order detection and to compute round-trip latencies. We measured typical RTTs robot-to-edge 12 ms and edge-to-server 4 ms in the hospital network; these numbers guided the design for acceptable update rates and timeouts.

The communication layer timestamps messages so that fusion algorithms can correctly account for delay $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$, modeled as $T_{\mathrm{RTT}} = T_{\mathrm{tx}} + T_{\mathrm{prop}} + T_{\mathrm{proc}} + T_{\mathrm{rx}}$ in our network tests, where measured average $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ was 16 ms in the hospital LAN.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section details the experimental protocol performed at Wongsonegoro Hospital, the metrics used to evaluate odometry calibration, and quantitative results including comparisons to baseline methods and ablation studies.

content.text: Experiments were performed in three corridor sections of Wongsonegoro Hospital approved by facility management, totaling 1200 calibration and validation runs collected over two weeks. The test environment includes typical hospital floor tiles, occasional foot traffic, and variable lighting. Ground truth was obtained via tape measure markers and waypoint logging from the hospital Map Server at known landmarks. Each calibration run consisted of a sequence of maneuvers: straight short (2 m), straight long (10 m), left turns of 90 degrees, and right turns of 90 degrees. Data acquisition included encoder ticks at 500 Hz, odometry outputs at 50 Hz, and camera snapshots for visual verification. Temperature and battery voltage were recorded to analyze environmental dependencies.
content.id_extra: Details of experimental parameters are in Table II and a photograph in Fig. 6.

content.text: We evaluate performance using translational RMSE, rotational drift per meter (deg/m), and an overall corridor tracking accuracy defined as the percentage of runs where final pose error is within 0.25 m and 2 degrees. The proposed method's quantitative results are summarized in Table III. For baseline comparisons we include Raw Odometry (vendor defaults), Wheel Radius Correction (single-parameter radius adjustment), Wheelbase Calibration (single-parameter baseline adjustment), and an EKF fusion baseline that uses raw odometry fused with sparse map waypoints.

Table III shows that the proposed OdometryCal-WG reduced translational RMSE to 0.124 m and rotational drift to 0.70 deg/m. These improvements lead to an overall corridor tracking accuracy of 95.4% on the test set. The average calibration latency measured on the Intel NUC was 12.3 ms, enabling near real-time updates during low-traffic windows. The translational RMSE numbers are computed over 1200 runs and are consistent with the confusion matrix and error histograms we produced for diagnostic purposes.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation

content.text: We compare the proposed method against several baselines and state-of-the-art approaches in Table IV. The baselines include a raw odometry baseline using vendor parameters, a single-parameter radius correction, a wheelbase-only calibration, and an EKF fusion method that aggregates odometry with sparse waypoint corrections. Our method consistently outperforms baselines in both accuracy and latency, demonstrating practical advantage in hospital deployments where compute resources are limited and calibration must be minimally intrusive.

Table IV demonstrates that the proposed method delivers the best trade-off between accuracy and latency among practical alternatives. The EKF fusion approach can reach competitive accuracy but at a significantly higher latency and greater reliance on external sensors. Ablation experiments in which we remove online updates or outlier rejection indicate a 1.8% drop in accuracy and an increase of translational RMSE to 0.187 m, confirming the value of each subsystem.

content.text: We conducted endurance tests consisting of a continuous 8-hour patrol along a fixed corridor loop to observe parameter drift and reliability under extended operation. The goal was to quantify drift accumulation rates and to test the ability of online updates to maintain calibration. Table V presents summarized endurance metrics, and Fig. 9 shows a time-series of translational RMSE over the 8-hour window. Results show that with online updates enabled, RMSE remained stable near 0.13 m, whereas without updates RMSE grew to 0.31 m after 8 hours.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We proposed OdometryCal-WG, a practical odometry calibration pipeline for differential-drive service robots operating in the real-world environment of Wongsonegoro Hospital, Semarang. The pipeline jointly estimates wheel radii and wheelbase parameters $p=[b, r_L, r_R]$ via constrained nonlinear least-squares and integrates online updates that adapt to slow environmental changes. Extensive experiments with 1200 runs and an 8-hour endurance test demonstrate that our method reduces translational RMSE from 0.462 m to 0.124 m and rotational drift from 2.6 deg/m to 0.70 deg/m, achieving 95.4% corridor tracking accuracy while running on readily available edge hardware with average latency 12.3 ms. These improvements materially enhance service performance for tasks such as medication delivery and patient guidance.

Despite achieving significant improvements, limitations remain. The approach still relies on occasional ground-truth waypoints for initial batch calibration, which requires minor staff involvement or pre-marked tape measures. Severe wheel slip events and abrupt surface changes can temporarily degrade accuracy until the online update accumulates sufficient data. Future work will explore automatic ground-truth acquisition using ceiling-mounted fiducials, incorporate tactile or force sensing to detect slip, and investigate lightweight learning-based residual models to handle rapidly changing floor conditions. We also plan to deploy the pipeline across additional hospital locations in Semarang to evaluate generalization and long-term maintenance demands.
